01.note: Rabbi Beroka Hoza'a often met Elijah the Prophet in the market of Bei Lefet and asked whether anyone there was worthy of the World-to-Come. Elijah said no, then pointed to a man in black shoes with no ritual fringes and said he was. The man, a Jewish prison guard, explained that he kept the men and women prisoners apart, risked his life to save Jewish women from gentiles, once splashed wine dregs on a betrothed girl's dress and claimed she was menstruating to protect her, and dressed like a gentile so he could warn the Sages of decrees. Elijah then pointed out two brothers as worthy too: they were jesters who cheered up the sad and made peace between people who quarreled.
01.why: The discussion has been telling of people Heaven honors, such as Abba, who quietly gave up his stolen rugs to charity; this story continues the theme that the worthiest people may be the least likely-looking.

people.name: Rabbi Beroka Hoza'a
people.about: A Sage often found in the market of Bei Lefet, to whom Elijah would appear.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The Prophet, who appears to Rabbi Beroka and points out who in the market is worthy of the World-to-Come.

terms.meaning: The life of reward after this world; to be 'worthy of the World-to-Come' is to have earned a share in it.
A dyed thread worn in the ritual fringes (tzitzit) on the corners of a garment, a visible sign of a Jewish man.

02.note: Ulla reported, in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak, an incident in which wolves swallowed two children and excreted them. The case came before the Sages, who ruled that the digested flesh was ritually pure but the bones were ritually impure.
02.why: The mishna lists a fast decreed because wolves had eaten two children; the Gemara adds this account of such an incident and the ruling it produced about the remains.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
people.about: The Sage in whose name Ulla reports it.

terms.meaning: A state, caused for example by contact with a human corpse, that bars a person or object from holy places and things. It is a religious status, not physical dirt.

03.note: In the days of Shimon ben Shetah, rain fell only on Tuesday nights and Friday nights. The crops grew enormous: wheat as big as kidneys, barley as big as olive pits, lentils like gold coins. People tied up samples and kept them for later generations, to show how much sin costs, citing Jeremiah's words that sins have withheld the good.
03.why: A teaching on the verse 'I will give your rains in their season' explains 'in their season' as Tuesday and Friday nights, when no one is out; this memory of Shimon ben Shetah's time is offered as proof.

people.name: Shimon ben Shetah
people.about: The leader in whose days the rain fell at these ideal times.

terms.meaning: A coin; here a gold one, used to describe the size of the lentils.

04.note: While the people were building the Temple in Herod's days, rain fell only at night. Each morning the wind blew, the clouds scattered, the sun came out and the people went back to work, so they knew that Heaven was helping the work of their hands.
04.why: This is a second example, after the days of Shimon ben Shetah, of rain falling 'in its season', at times when it does no harm.

people.name: Herod
people.about: The king in whose days the Temple was being built.

05.note: Late in the month of Adar with no rain, the people asked Honi HaMe'aggel to pray. When his prayer failed, he drew a circle, stood in it and swore by God's name not to leave until God had mercy. A trickle came; his students said it was too little. He asked for more and it poured violently, drops the size of a barrel's mouth. He asked for rain of blessing and it fell normally, but so much that the people fled up to the Temple Mount. He said one does not pray over an excess of good, yet he brought a thanks-offering and asked that the rain stop. At once the sun came out. Shimon ben Shetah sent word that if he were not Honi, he would have decreed ostracism on him for risking the desecration of God's name.
05.why: The mishna mentions in passing that people once sent to Honi to pray for rain; the Gemara now gives the full account, as the Sages taught it.

people.name: Honi HaMe'aggel
people.about: A man whose prayers for rain were answered; the people send to him in a drought.

people.name: Shimon ben Shetah
people.about: A leading Sage who rebukes Honi for his oath.

people.name: Habakkuk
people.about: The prophet whose way of standing in a circle Honi copies.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet held the keys of rain and swore it would not fall, so Honi's oath could have clashed with his.

terms.meaning: A sacrifice brought to thank God; here a bull, on whose head Honi lays his hands while praying.
A formal ban by the Sages that cut a person off from the community until he repented.
A liquid measure, used here to show how huge each raindrop was.

05.flag: The story stops mid-sentence in Shimon ben Shetah's message; its second half ('what can I do to you...') sits in the next segment.

06.note: Honi was troubled all his life by the verse comparing Israel's seventy-year exile to a dream: can anyone sleep seventy years? One day he met a man planting a carob tree that would take seventy years to bear fruit; the man said he was planting for his descendants as his ancestors had planted for him. Honi sat to eat, fell asleep, and was hidden by a rock formation for seventy years. He woke to find the planter's grandson picking carobs. At home and in the study hall no one believed he was Honi or gave him proper respect. Upset, he prayed for mercy and died. Rava drew the folk saying: either friendship or death.
06.why: The Sages have just praised Honi for saving his generation through prayer; Rabbi Yohanan adds a second story about the same righteous man.

people.name: Honi HaMe'aggel
people.about: The righteous man whose prayer brought rain; here he sleeps seventy years.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage who tells the story.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who links the story to a folk saying.

terms.meaning: A slow-growing tree with edible pods; the text says this one would take seventy years to bear fruit.
The house of study where the Sages met to learn and discuss Torah.

07.note: Abba Hilkiyya, Honi's grandson, was a day laborer whose prayers brought rain. Two Sages sent to him found him hoeing; he ignored their greeting, carried wood on one shoulder and his cloak on the other, went barefoot except in water, lifted his clothes in thorns did not invite them to eat, and gave his younger child twice the bread. On the roof he and his wife prayed, and clouds came first from her corner. He explained it all: a hired man may not pause work; the cloak was borrowed; skin heals but cloth does not; the Sages were strangers to him; there was too little bread; the younger child studied all day. His wife's prayer came first because her charity, bread, helped at once, and because she had prayed that some hooligans would repent while he prayed that they would die. They repented.
07.why: It continues stories about Honi's family; the Gemara introduces Abba Hilkiyya as Honi's grandson, and like Honi he is someone the Sages turn to when rain is needed.

people.name: Abba Hilkiyya
people.about: Honi HaMe'aggel's grandson, a day laborer to whom the Sages sent when rain was needed.

people.name: Honi HaMe'aggel
people.about: Abba Hilkiyya's grandfather.

terms.meaning: A worker hired by the day, whose time belongs to his employer; this is why he would not stop to return a greeting.

08.note: When rain was needed, Rabbi Yona, the father of Rabbi Mani, would tell his household to give him his sack so he could go buy grain. Instead he went to a low, secluded place, covered himself in sackcloth and prayed, and rain came. When he returned home empty-handed and they asked about the grain, he said that since rain had come, things would now get easier in the world.
08.why: Rabbi Zerika contrasts the pious men of Babylonia, who gather publicly to pray for rain, with the powerful men of the Land of Israel; Rabbi Yona is his example of praying in secret.

people.name: Rabbi Yona
people.about: The father of Rabbi Mani; one of the 'powerful men of the Land of Israel' whose prayers brought rain.

terms.meaning: Rough cloth worn as a sign of mourning or distress during prayer and fasting.

09.note: Rabbi Mani, Rabbi Yona's son, was being persecuted by members of the house of the Nasi. He threw himself down on his father's grave and cried: Father, Father, these men are persecuting me. One day the men rode past the grave, and their horses' legs stuck fast in the ground until they promised to stop persecuting him.
09.why: The Gemara has just told how Rabbi Yona's hidden prayers brought rain; it adds that his power continued after his death, answering his son at his grave.

people.name: Rabbi Mani
people.about: Rabbi Yona's son, persecuted by members of the house of the Nasi.

people.name: Rabbi Yona
people.about: Rabbi Mani's father, at whose grave Rabbi Mani prays.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel; 'the house of the Nasi' means his family and circle.

10.note: Rabbi Mani often sat before Rabbi Yitzhak ben Elyashiv. When he complained that the wealthy members of his father-in-law's family were persecuting him, Rabbi Yitzhak said, 'May they become poor,' and they did. When they then pressed him for support, Rabbi Yitzhak said, 'May they become rich,' and they did. When Rabbi Mani complained that his wife, Hana, was not pleasing to him, Rabbi Yitzhak said, 'Let Hana grow beautiful,' and she did. When she then acted haughtily toward him, Rabbi Yitzhak said, 'Let Hana return to her plain looks,' and she did.
10.why: It is the next in a run of stories about Rabbi Mani and the wonders done for him, after his father's grave saved him from his persecutors.

people.name: Rabbi Mani
people.about: Rabbi Yona's son, who brings his troubles to Rabbi Yitzhak ben Elyashiv.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak ben Elyashiv
people.about: A miracle worker before whom Rabbi Mani often sat; whatever he says comes true.

people.name: Hana
people.about: Rabbi Mani's wife.

11.note: Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat hired laborers for his field but came late and brought them no food. Starving, they complained to his son, and the son told a fig tree to yield its fruit for his father's workers. It did, and they ate. When the father arrived and apologized, explaining he had been delayed by a mitzva, the workers blessed him: may God satisfy you as your son satisfied us. Hearing what had happened, he told his son that since he had troubled his Creator to make a fig bear fruit out of season, he would be taken before his time. And indeed, his son died young.
11.why: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin had told Rav Ashi he left Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat because the man showed no mercy even to his own son; the Gemara asks what happened with the son and tells this story.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat
people.about: A Sage, whose student said he had no mercy even on his own children.

terms.meaning: A religious commandment, or a good deed done to fulfill one.

12.note: Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat had a very beautiful daughter. One day he saw a man making a hole in the hedge to look at her. When Rabbi Yosei asked what he was doing, the man said that if he had not merited marrying her, could he not at least merit looking at her? Rabbi Yosei then said to his daughter: You are causing people distress; return to your dust, and let people no longer stumble into sin because of you. The text does not say what happened next.
12.why: This answers the Gemara's question about the second half of Rabbi Yosei bar Avin's complaint, that his teacher had no mercy even on his daughter.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat
people.about: A Sage said by his student to have no mercy on his own children.

13.note: Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat had a donkey that people hired by the day. Each evening they sent it home with its hire money on its back, and it walked to its owner's house. If they put on too much or too little money, it would not go. Once someone forgot a pair of sandals on it, and it would not move until they took them off.
13.why: After the stories of his son and daughter, the Gemara tells one more about Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat, in which even his donkey refuses to carry what is not owed.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat
people.about: The donkey's owner.

14.note: Elazar of Birta gave charity collectors everything he had on him, so they hid when they saw him. One day, going to the market to buy his daughter's dowry, he spotted them hiding and ran after them. They said they were collecting for the wedding of an orphan boy and girl, and he swore by the Temple service that these came before his daughter. He gave them everything and bought wheat with the one coin he had left, tossing it into his granary. When his wife went to open the granary, it was so full of wheat that the door would not open. His daughter ran to tell him what God had done, but he swore that the wheat was consecrated, and she could have no more of it than any poor person.
14.why: The Gemara is gathering stories of miracles done for righteous people; this one follows the stories of Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat.

people.name: Elazar of Birta
people.about: A man who gave the charity collectors everything he had on him.

terms.meaning: The money and goods a bride brings into her marriage, provided by her family.
The sacred worship in the Temple; Elazar swears by it.
Dedicated to holy use, so it may not be used privately; Elazar declares the wheat so as far as his daughter is concerned.

15.note: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia decreed a fast and prayed, but no rain came. He lamented how far he, Yehuda ben Gamliel, fell short of the prophet Samuel of Rama, and cried woe to the generation stuck with such a leader and woe to the one in whose days this happened. He became upset, and the rain came.
15.why: After a run of miracle stories, the Gemara returns to its topic, fasting for rain, and tells of leaders whose fasts at first brought nothing.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: A leader who decrees a fast for rain; he calls himself Yehuda ben Gamliel.

people.name: Samuel of Rama
people.about: The prophet Samuel, whom Rabbi Yehuda Nesia compares himself to.

terms.meaning: In a drought, community leaders could declare a public fast day of prayer asking God for rain.

16.note: The house of the Nasi decreed a fast, but no rain came. Oshaya, the youngest of the group of Sages, taught a verse that calls the leaders the 'eyes' of the congregation, and a parable: if a bride's eyes are beautiful, there is no need to check the rest of her, but if her eyes are bleary, her whole body must be checked. The Nasi's servants put a scarf around his neck and tormented him. His townspeople told them to let him be: he pains us too with his rebukes, but since all he does is for Heaven's sake, we let him be.
16.why: This is the second of two stories about fasts declared by the house of the Nasi; here no rain comes, and Oshaya hints that the leaders themselves are to blame.

people.name: Oshaya
people.about: The youngest of the group of Sages, who rebukes the house of the Nasi.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel; 'the house of the Nasi' means his household and court.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

17.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi decreed a fast, but no rain came. Ilfa (some say Rabbi Ilfi) led the prayers before him. When he said 'Who makes the wind blow,' the wind blew; when he said 'Who makes the rain fall,' the rain came. Asked what his good deeds were, he said he lived in a poor town with no wine for kiddush or havdala, and he took the trouble to bring wine so the people could fulfill their duty.
17.why: It is one in a series of stories about fasts for rain where a leader's fast fails until someone else's merit brings the rain.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who decreed the fast.

people.name: Ilfa
people.about: The man who led the prayers (some say Rabbi Ilfi); he brings wine to his poor town.

terms.meaning: Blessings, usually said over a cup of wine, that mark the start (kiddush) and end (havdala) of Shabbat and festivals.

terms.term: He Who makes the wind blow
terms.meaning: Words from the daily standing prayer praising God as the giver of wind and rain.

18.note: Rav came to a certain place, decreed a fast, but no rain came. The prayer leader went before the ark; when he said 'Who makes the wind blow,' the wind blew, and when he said 'Who makes the rain fall,' the rain came. Rav asked what his good deeds were. He said he taught Bible to poor children as to rich ones, took nothing from those who could not pay, and kept a fishpond so he could coax any child who neglected his lessons with fish until he came back to read.
18.why: The Gemara pairs it with the story just told about Ilfa: again a fast fails and an ordinary prayer leader's good deeds bring the rain.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who decreed the fast in that place.

terms.meaning: The person who leads the congregation in public prayer.

19.note: Rav Nahman decreed a fast and prayed, but no rain came. He said: Take Nahman and throw him from the wall to the ground. He became upset, and the rain came.
19.why: It continues the series of fasts for rain that fail at first; here, as with Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, the leader's own distress brings the rain.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage who decreed a fast for rain.

20.note: Rav Yehuda saw two people wasting bread and concluded that there was plenty in the world. He cast his eyes on it, and there was a famine. The Sages asked his attendant, Rav Kahana son of Rav Nehunya, to get him to leave by the door near the market. There he saw a crowd around a single container of dates for sale and understood there was famine. He told his attendant to remove his shoes; when one shoe came off, rain came. As he was about to remove the other, Elijah came and told him God's words: if you remove the other one, I will destroy the world.
20.why: Rabba has just said that in Rav Yehuda's time, rain came as soon as he took off one shoe; the Gemara tells the story behind that remark.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage whose look causes a famine and whose distress brings rain.

people.name: Rav Kahana son of Rav Nehunya
people.about: Rav Yehuda's attendant.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who brings Rav Yehuda God's message.

terms.meaning: Going barefoot was a sign of distress and fasting.
